headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, ONS says

terms.meaning: The total value of goods and services an economy produces.
A comparison with the previous three-month period.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, ONS says
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter of 2026, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 12 November. The figure covers July to September and is measured as gross domestic product (GDP), seasonally adjusted and compared with the previous quarter.
The ONS shows growth of 0.5% in the second quarter and 0.6% in the first, so the latest figure is the strongest of the three. CNBC reported that artificial intelligence is providing an 'extra engine of growth'. The ONS puts the size of the economy in the quarter at about £798bn in current prices.
The next GDP release is due on 22 December, with the monthly estimate for October on 11 December. The figures arrive as the Bank of England has warned about inflation and raised interest rates, so the strength of growth will matter to its next decision.
levels.why: Strong growth affects jobs, wages, tax receipts and how far the Bank of England feels it must go on interest rates.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in July to September
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September 2026, the Office for National Statistics reported on 12 November. That is gross domestic product, or GDP, compared with the previous three months and adjusted for seasonal patterns.
Growth was 0.5% in the second quarter and 0.6% in the first, so this is the fastest of the three. CNBC said artificial intelligence is acting as an 'extra engine of growth'. In current prices the economy was worth about £798bn over the quarter.
The next full GDP figures come on 22 December, and the monthly figure for October on 11 December. Those will show whether the pace is holding as the Bank of England weighs further interest rate rises to tackle inflation.
levels.why: It gives an early read on whether the economy can cope with higher interest rates and energy costs.

levels.headline: UK economy expands 0.7% as growth picks up
levels.body:
Official figures show the UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter of 2026, from July to September. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) published the first estimate on 12 November. Growth is measured by GDP, the value of everything the country produces, compared with the quarter before.
That beats the 0.5% recorded in the second quarter and 0.6% in the first. CNBC reported that artificial intelligence is giving the economy an 'extra engine of growth'. Over the quarter the economy produced about £798bn of goods and services.
More data follows soon: monthly GDP for October on 11 December and the next quarterly estimate on 22 December. The Bank of England will be watching, because it is trying to bring down inflation without choking growth.
levels.why: Growth shapes jobs and public finances, and it guides how much the Bank of England thinks it can raise interest rates.

levels.headline: UK economy grows by 0.7% in third quarter
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the three months from July to September, according to the Office for National Statistics. It said on 12 November that gross domestic product, the main measure of the economy's size, rose by that amount compared with the previous quarter.
The previous two quarters were weaker: growth was 0.5% in the second quarter and 0.6% in the first. CNBC said artificial intelligence is helping drive the expansion, describing it as an 'extra engine of growth'. The economy produced roughly £798bn in the quarter.
The next releases are on 11 December and 22 December. Economists will use them to judge whether the Bank of England can keep raising interest rates without damaging the recovery.
levels.why: Stronger growth can mean more jobs and tax income, but it also affects interest rate decisions.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew 0.7% from July to September
levels.body:
The UK economy got bigger by 0.7% between July and September. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, shared the news on 12 November. It measures the economy with something called GDP, which means the total value of what everyone in the country makes and sells, including goods and services.
Growth was 0.5% in the spring and 0.6% at the start of the year, so this is the best of the three. CNBC reported that artificial intelligence is helping, calling it an 'extra engine of growth'. In all, the economy produced about £798bn.
More figures come on 11 and 22 December. The Bank of England will study them when it decides whether to put interest rates up again to control prices.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and more money for public services, which affects ordinary families.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew by 0.7% in three months
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September. The Office for National Statistics shared the figure on 12 November. Growth means the country made and sold more than it did in the three months before.
Experts measure this with GDP, which adds up the value of everything produced, such as cars, haircuts and computer services. Earlier this year growth was smaller: 0.5% in spring and 0.6% in the first three months. A news report said artificial intelligence is giving the economy an 'extra engine of growth'.
The next numbers are due in December. The Bank of England will look at them, because it sets interest rates, which change how much it costs to borrow money.
levels.why: When the economy grows, there can be more jobs and more money for things like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The UK economy got bigger by 0.7%
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% over the summer. That covers July, August and September. The people who count these things, the Office for National Statistics, told us on 12 November.
An economy is all the things people in a country make, sell and buy. GDP is the name for its total value. When GDP goes up, the country is making more. Earlier in the year it went up by less: 0.5% in spring and 0.6% at the start of the year.
One report said new computer technology called artificial intelligence is helping. More figures come in December. The Bank of England will use them to decide about interest rates, which affect the cost of loans.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs, but the Bank of England also watches it when it sets interest rates.

levels.headline: The country made and sold more this summer
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% over the summer months, from July to September. A group called the Office for National Statistics counted everything and told us on 12 November.
The economy means all the things people in the country make, sell and buy, like food, phones and bus rides. When the total goes up, we say the economy has grown. Growth was smaller earlier in the year, at 0.5% and then 0.6%.
One news report said a kind of smart computer technology called AI is helping the economy grow. The Bank of England will look at the numbers before deciding about interest rates. Those are the extra fees people pay when they borrow money.
levels.why: More growth can mean more jobs and more money for things the country needs.

levels.headline: The UK made more stuff this summer
levels.body:
The UK grew a little bigger this summer. The country made and sold more things between July and September. People who count this told us on 12 November. They said it grew by 0.7%. That means 7 extra pounds for every 1,000 pounds before.
The economy is all the things a country makes and sells, such as food, toys and haircuts. Earlier this year it grew by less. A news report said clever computer helpers, called AI, are helping.
A group called the Bank of England sets the price of borrowing money. That price is called interest. It will look at these numbers soon, to decide what to do next.
levels.why: When the country makes more, there can be more jobs for people.

levels.headline: The country had a good summer for making things
levels.body:
Imagine the whole country is one big school fair. People make cakes, crafts and games, and they sell them. If more things are made and sold than last time, the fair has grown.
That is what happened to the UK this summer. Between July and September, the country made and sold a bit more, about 7 extra pounds for every 1,000 pounds it made before. The grown-ups who count this told us on 12 November. They are called the Office for National Statistics.
A news report said clever computers, called AI, are helping. Another group, the Bank of England, looks after the price of borrowing money, a bit like a school rule about lending pocket money. It will look at these numbers soon.
levels.why: A bigger fair can mean more jobs and more money for the things we all share.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.4% at 7,561.67 as Nvidia slides, but posts best week since August

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 of the largest companies listed in the US.
An index dominated by technology companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.4% at 7,561.67 as Nvidia slides, but posts best week since August
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November, the last completed trading session. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.91% to 25,136.27, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 50.46 points, or 0.1%, to 52,347.55, according to CNBC.
Nvidia shares fell 2% on Friday, extending a drop of more than 4% the day before, after the exit of founder and chief executive Jensen Huang. HSBC also downgraded the chipmaker to hold. The company's board had opened an investigation into his relationship with a businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
Despite Friday's falls, CNBC said all three indexes had their best weekly performance since early August. The S&P 500 gained 2.5% over the week, the Nasdaq 2.3% and the Dow 2.1%.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and investment funds, and Nvidia's turmoil shows how reliant markets are on a few big technology firms.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends Friday mixed as S&P 500 slips 0.4% and Nvidia falls
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November, the most recent completed session. The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.91% to finish at 25,136.27, but the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.1%, or 50.46 points, to 52,347.55, CNBC reported.
Nvidia fell 2% after dropping more than 4% the previous day, following the departure of chief executive Jensen Huang. HSBC downgraded the shares to hold. Nvidia's board had been investigating his relationship with a businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies describe as a Chinese spy.
The day was weak, but the week was strong. CNBC said it was the best week for all three main indexes since early August, with the S&P 500 up 2.5%, the Nasdaq up 2.3% and the Dow up 2.1%.
levels.why: Moves in US shares feed through to UK pension funds and global markets.

levels.headline: US stocks end the week higher despite Friday dip
levels.body:
The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big US companies, closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November. The Nasdaq, which is heavy with tech firms, fell 0.91% to 25,136.27. The Dow Jones, which follows 30 major companies, rose 0.1% to 52,347.55, CNBC reported.
Chipmaker Nvidia was the main drag. Its shares fell 2% on Friday after dropping more than 4% on Thursday, when chief executive Jensen Huang left the company. Bank HSBC also cut its rating to hold.
Still, it was a good week overall. CNBC said it was the best week for all three indexes since early August. The S&P 500 rose 2.5%, the Nasdaq 2.3% and the Dow 2.1%.
levels.why: US share prices influence savings and pensions around the world.

levels.headline: S&P 500 falls 0.4% on Friday but ends the week up 2.5%
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down 0.4% at 7,561.67 on Friday 13 November, the latest finished trading day. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.91% to 25,136.27, and the Dow Jones rose 0.1% to 52,347.55, according to CNBC.
Shares in chipmaker Nvidia fell 2% after a drop of more than 4% the day before. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, stepped down on Thursday amid questions about his links to a woman US officials call a Chinese spy. HSBC also downgraded the stock to hold.
Over the whole week, though, markets did well. CNBC said it was the best week since early August: the S&P 500 gained 2.5%, the Nasdaq 2.3% and the Dow 2.1%.
levels.why: What happens on Wall Street can affect pension pots and the cost of borrowing far beyond the US.

levels.headline: US shares dip on Friday but have a good week
levels.body:
The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big US companies, and its value went down by 0.4% on Friday 13 November. It ended at 7,561.67. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology firms, fell by 0.91%. The Dow Jones, another list of big companies, rose slightly, by 0.1%.
The main worry was Nvidia, a company that makes computer chips. Its shares fell 2% after a bigger fall the day before. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, left the job on Thursday after reports about his links to a woman that US officials say is a spy for China.
Even so, the week was good. CNBC said it was the best since early August. The S&P 500 rose 2.5% over the five days.
levels.why: Share prices can change the value of savings and pensions for millions of people.

levels.headline: US share prices ended Friday a little lower
levels.body:
The main US share index, the S&P 500, ended Friday 13 November down 0.4%, at 7,561.67. Shares are small pieces of companies, and an index is a list that shows how a group of them is doing. The Nasdaq, full of technology firms, fell 0.91%, while the Dow Jones, a list of 30 large companies, rose 0.1%.
The chip maker Nvidia was the main worry. Its shares fell 2% after a bigger drop the day before, when its chief executive, Jensen Huang, left. Reports linked him to a woman US officials call a Chinese spy.
The week as a whole was strong. CNBC said it was the best since early August, with the S&P 500 up 2.5% over the week.
levels.why: Many pensions and savings are invested in shares, so price moves can matter to ordinary people.

levels.headline: US share prices fell a little on Friday
levels.body:
On Friday 13 November, share prices in the US went down a little. The main list of big companies, called the S&P 500, fell by 0.4%. A list full of technology firms, the Nasdaq, fell by almost 1%. A third list, the Dow Jones, went up by a tiny 0.1%.
A big computer chip company called Nvidia had a bad day. Its shares fell 2%. The day before, the boss, Jensen Huang, had left his job. There were reports about his link to a woman US officials think is a spy for China.
But the whole week was good for shares. They went up about 2% or 3%. That was the best week since early August.
levels.why: Share prices matter because many people's savings and pensions are invested in them.

levels.headline: Share prices in the US went down a bit on Friday
levels.body:
A share is a tiny piece of a company. People buy shares hoping the company does well. On Friday 13 November, prices of shares in big US companies went down a bit. A well-known list called the S&P 500 dropped by 0.4%.
A company called Nvidia, which makes computer chips, had a bad day. Its boss, Jensen Huang, left his job on Thursday. News reports said he had been close to a woman that US officials think is a spy. Nvidia shares fell 2%.
But the whole week was good, with prices up about 2% to 3%. It was the best week since early August. Many people have savings that are invested in shares.
levels.why: Many pensions and savings rise or fall with share prices.

levels.headline: Share prices dipped on Friday but rose over the week
levels.body:
Shares are small pieces of companies. Their prices go up and down every day. On Friday 13 November, prices for big US companies dipped a little. One main list, the S&P 500, went down by 0.4%.
One company, Nvidia, which makes computer chips, was in the news. Its boss, Jensen Huang, left his job. People worried, so some sold their shares, and the price fell.
But look at the whole week. Prices went up by about 2 or 3 pounds in every 100. That was the best week since early August. A dip on one day is not the whole story.
levels.why: Many families have savings in shares, so price changes can matter to them.

levels.headline: Prices of shares wobbled on Friday
levels.body:
Shares are tiny slices of a company. If you own a slice, you own a bit of the company. Their prices wobble up and down, a bit like a seesaw in the playground.
On Friday 13 November, the seesaw tipped down a little for big US companies. A company called Nvidia, which makes computer chips, had a bad day because its boss left his job. Some people sold their slices, so the price went down.
But over the whole week the seesaw went up. Prices rose by a few pennies in every pound, the best week since early August. One wobbly day does not mean the whole week was bad.
levels.why: Many grown-ups save in shares, so wobbles can matter to them.

headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% and warns inflation could near 5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences borrowing costs.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% and warns inflation could near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on 5 November, its first increase in more than three years. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8 to 1, with the one dissenter wanting a half-point rise.
The Bank warned that inflation, which reached 3.5% in September, an 11-month high, could rise towards 5% by mid-2027. The energy shock linked to the US-Iran war is the main driver. The Bank's target is 2%.
CNBC reported that unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, this may not be the last rise. Markets put the chance of another increase at the next meeting, on 17 December, at about 73%, according to LSEG data.
levels.why: Higher Bank Rate raises costs for mortgage holders and businesses, but is meant to bring prices under control.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts rates to 4% as inflation threatens to near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England put its main interest rate up by 0.25 percentage points to 4% on 5 November, the first rise in over three years. Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee backed it. One wanted a bigger half-point increase.
The Bank said inflation, at 3.5% in September, could climb towards 5% by mid-2027, well above its 2% target. The energy shock tied to the US-Iran war is the main cause.
CNBC reported that the rise may not be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved. LSEG data shows markets see about a 73% chance of another rise at the meeting on 17 December.
levels.why: Interest rate decisions change what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% on 5 November, up from 3.75%. It was the first rise in more than three years. Eight members voted for it and one wanted a larger rise of half a percentage point.
The Bank also warned that inflation, the speed at which prices rise, could approach 5% by the middle of 2027. It was 3.5% in September. The Bank aims for 2%. Higher energy costs linked to the war involving Iran are the main reason.
CNBC said more rises are possible if the conflict continues. Financial markets think there is about a 73% chance of another increase on 17 December.
levels.why: It affects the cost of mortgages and loans, and is the Bank's main tool for slowing price rises.

levels.headline: Bank of England puts up interest rates and warns of higher prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate to 4%, up a quarter of a percentage point. The decision on 5 November was the first rise for over three years. Eight members voted for it, and one wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank is worried about inflation, which measures how fast prices go up. It was 3.5% in September, and the Bank thinks it could near 5% by the middle of 2027. Its target is 2%. Higher energy prices because of the war with Iran are a big reason.
Markets think another rise on 17 December is quite likely, at around 73%, according to data from LSEG.
levels.why: Higher rates make borrowing dearer for households and firms, but aim to stop prices rising too fast.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to try to slow rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. It announced the change on 5 November. It is the first rise for more than three years. Interest is the price of borrowing money, and the Bank's rate affects what people pay on mortgages and loans.
The Bank did this because prices are rising too fast. Inflation, the rate prices go up by, was 3.5% in September. The Bank wants it near 2%. It fears it could reach nearly 5% by mid-2027, mostly because energy costs have jumped during the war involving Iran.
Markets think there may be another rise on 17 December.
levels.why: This matters because many people's mortgage payments and savings rates follow the Bank's decisions.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has raised interest rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up interest rates to 4%. It said so on 5 November. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. The Bank's rate guides what banks charge for loans and mortgages.
Why did it do this? Prices are going up too fast. This is called inflation. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. The Bank wants that closer to 2%. It thinks it could reach almost 5% in 2027. Energy has become more expensive because of a war involving Iran.
Some people may pay more on their loans. Others may earn more on savings. The Bank may raise rates again in December.
levels.why: The decision can change what families pay each month on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: The Bank of England made borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%. It told everyone on 5 November. It is the first rise for over three years.
Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow. If you borrow 100 pounds and the rate is 4%, you pay back 4 pounds more each year. Banks follow the Bank of England, so loans and mortgages can cost more now.
Why do this? Prices are going up too fast. It is called inflation. Things cost 3.5% more than last year, and the Bank thinks it could be nearly 5% soon. Oil and gas have become dearer because of a war. Higher interest can slow prices down. Another rise is possible in December.
levels.why: It can change what families pay on loans, and it aims to stop prices going up too fast.

levels.headline: The Bank has made loans cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a very important bank. It has made borrowing money cost more. It did this on 5 November.
When you borrow money, you pay back a bit extra. That extra is called interest. The Bank of England sets a main rate, and other banks follow it. Now the rate is 4%. Before, it was a little lower.
Why? Prices are going up quite fast. This is called inflation. Food, fuel and other things cost more than before. A war far away has made oil and gas dearer. When borrowing costs more, people spend less, and prices can slow down. The Bank might do it again in December.
levels.why: If loans cost more, families with mortgages may have less money to spend.

levels.headline: The Bank of England made borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up the cost of borrowing. It said so on 5 November. The grown-ups who run it were worried that prices are going up too fast.
Think of borrowing money like borrowing a toy for a week and giving back the toy plus a little extra. That little extra is called interest. Now it is a bit bigger.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less. Then shops stop putting their prices up so fast. Things like petrol and gas have cost more because of a war far away. That is why prices have risen. The Bank may make borrowing cost more again in December.
levels.why: It can mean families who borrow money pay a bit more each month.

levels.headline: The Bank of England made borrowing cost a bit more
levels.body:
The Bank of England is like a head teacher for the country's money. It has made a new rule. Borrowing money now costs a little more. It said so on 5 November.
Imagine you borrow a pound from a friend, and you give back a pound and a few pennies. Those extra pennies are called interest. Now the extra pennies are a bit bigger.
Why did it do this? Prices in the shops are going up quite fast. A war far away has made oil and gas cost more, and that makes lots of things cost more. When borrowing is dearer, people buy a little less, and prices stop climbing so quickly. The Bank might do it again in December.
levels.why: If borrowing costs more, families who owe money may have less to spend.

headline: Hot US inflation data raises bets on Federal Reserve rate rise in December

terms.meaning: The central bank of the United States.
The return on US government borrowing, which shapes loan costs.

levels.headline: Hot US inflation data raises bets on Federal Reserve rate rise in December
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October compared with September, above the 0.3% economists had expected. The reading pushed the 10-year Treasury yield up by nearly 10 basis points to 4.95%, according to CNBC.
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September, its first increase since 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. It held in October. Traders widely expect it to raise rates again when it meets in December.
CME's FedWatch tool put the chance of a quarter-point rise at 88% and of a half-point rise at 11%. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said more rises would not necessarily be a policy error. Long-term yields are around their highest since 2002.
levels.why: US interest rates influence global borrowing costs, the value of the dollar and share prices worldwide.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than forecast, lifting bets on a December rate rise
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% forecast, CNBC reported. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped nearly 10 basis points to 4.95% after the figures.
The Federal Reserve lifted rates in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first rise since 2023, then held in October. Markets expect another increase when it meets in December.
According to CME's FedWatch tool, there is an 88% chance of a quarter-point rise and 11% of a half-point rise. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said further rises would not necessarily be a mistake. Long-dated yields are near their highest since 2002.
levels.why: The Fed's decisions ripple through mortgage rates, exchange rates and markets across the world.

levels.headline: US inflation comes in hotter than expected
levels.body:
Prices in the United States rose 0.4% in October compared with the month before. Economists had expected 0.3%. After the news, the yield on 10-year US government bonds rose to 4.95%, CNBC reported.
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, raised interest rates in September to between 3.75% and 4%. That was its first rise since 2023. It kept rates the same in October, but traders expect another rise in December.
The CME's FedWatch tool shows an 88% chance of a quarter-point rise and an 11% chance of a half-point rise. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said more rises are not necessarily a mistake.
levels.why: US rates affect borrowing costs and markets around the world, including in the UK.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than expected, so interest rates may go up again
levels.body:
US prices rose 0.4% in October, faster than the 0.3% experts had predicted. As a result, the interest the US government pays to borrow for ten years rose to 4.95%, CNBC reported.
The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, raised its interest rate in September to between 3.75% and 4%. It had not done that since 2023. It held the rate in October, but many traders now expect a rise in December.
A tool called FedWatch suggests an 88% chance of a small rise and an 11% chance of a bigger one. The Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, says more rises would not necessarily be a mistake.
levels.why: America's interest rates affect borrowing costs for people and companies around the world.

levels.headline: Prices in the US are rising faster, so interest rates may go up
levels.body:
Prices in the United States went up by 0.4% in October. Experts had thought they would rise by 0.3%. That is a sign that inflation, the speed at which prices rise, is staying high.
The US central bank is called the Federal Reserve. It sets the main interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It put the rate up in September to between 3.75% and 4%. In October it left it alone. Now many traders think it will raise it again in December. One tool says the chance of a small rise is 88%.
The interest the US government pays on its ten-year loans rose to 4.95% after the news.
levels.why: US interest rates can change borrowing costs and prices around the world.

levels.headline: US prices are rising faster, so the central bank may raise rates again
levels.body:
Prices in the US rose by 0.4% in October. Experts had expected 0.3%. This is called inflation: the speed at which prices go up. It is still too high for the US central bank, the Federal Reserve.
The Fed controls the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. It raised the rate in September and left it alone in October. After the new figures, many traders think it will raise it again in December. They put the chance of a small rise at 88%.
The US government also borrows money. The interest it pays on ten-year loans rose to 4.95% after the news.
levels.why: US interest rates can change borrowing costs for families and firms in other countries too.

levels.headline: US prices rose faster than expected
levels.body:
Prices in the United States went up by 0.4% in October. People who study the economy thought it would be 0.3%. So prices are going up faster than hoped.
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets the price of borrowing money, called the interest rate. It raised the rate in September. It then left it alone in October. Now many people who trade in money think it will raise it again in December. They think a small rise is very likely.
The US government also borrows money. The price it pays to borrow for ten years rose to 4.95% after the news.
levels.why: US interest rates can affect the cost of borrowing in other countries.

levels.headline: US prices are going up faster than people hoped
levels.body:
Prices in the United States rose by 0.4% in October. That is faster than the 0.3% that experts expected.
The US has a central bank called the Fed. It decides how much it costs to borrow money. That cost is called the interest rate. Last month it left the rate alone. In September it raised it. Now many people think it will raise it again in December, because prices are going up too fast.
The US government also borrows money, and it has to pay interest. After the news, that interest went up a bit, to 4.95%.
What happens in the US can change prices and loans in other countries too.
levels.why: The US is a huge economy, so its interest rates can affect families far away.

levels.headline: Prices in America went up faster than people thought
levels.body:
Prices in America went up by 0.4% in October. Experts thought they would go up by 0.3%. So things cost a bit more than hoped.
America has a big bank for the whole country, called the Fed. It decides how much extra you pay when you borrow money. That extra is called interest. The Fed put interest up in September. Now many people think it will put it up again in December, to make prices slow down.
When prices rise too fast, a rise in interest can help, because people spend a bit less. America is a very big country, so what it does can matter for other places too.
levels.why: It matters because America's rates can change borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: Things in America cost a bit more than people thought
levels.body:
Imagine the price of a sticker goes up faster than anyone expected. That is what happened to lots of things in America. In October, prices went up by 0.4%. Grown-ups who study this thought it would be 0.3%.
America has a big bank for the whole country, called the Fed. It decides how much extra you pay when you borrow money, a bit like paying back a pound plus a few pennies. Those extra pennies are called interest.
Many people now think the Fed will make the extra pennies bigger in December. That would help stop prices going up so quickly. America is big, so this can matter to other countries too.
levels.why: It could change how much people and countries pay to borrow money.

headline: UK and EU issue joint statement on Withdrawal Agreement, pointing to summit on 20 November

terms.meaning: The 2020 treaty setting the terms of the UK's exit from the EU.
The arrangements for trade involving Northern Ireland.

levels.headline: UK and EU issue joint statement on Withdrawal Agreement, pointing to summit on 20 November
levels.body:
The UK and the European Union published a joint statement on 10 November after a meeting of the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee. The committee oversees how the Withdrawal Agreement, the treaty covering the UK's exit from the EU, is put into practice.
The statement covers implementation of the Withdrawal Agreement and of the Windsor Framework, the arrangements governing trade involving Northern Ireland. It also points to an EU-UK Summit on 20 November 2026.
The GOV.UK page does not set out what the summit will decide. The joint committee is a routine part of the relationship: it meets to check that both sides are meeting their obligations under the deal agreed in 2020.
levels.why: How the UK and EU work together affects trade, travel and Northern Ireland, and so costs and rules for businesses and people.

levels.headline: UK and EU meet on Brexit deal and point to summit on 20 November
levels.body:
The UK and the EU issued a joint statement on 10 November after a meeting of the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee, the body that oversees the Brexit divorce treaty.
The statement concerns putting the Withdrawal Agreement and the Windsor Framework into effect. The Windsor Framework sets the rules for trade involving Northern Ireland. The statement also refers to an EU-UK Summit on 20 November 2026.
The GOV.UK page does not say what the summit will decide. Joint committee meetings are routine checks that both sides are keeping to the agreement made in 2020.
levels.why: The relationship with the EU shapes trade, travel and Northern Ireland's rules.

levels.headline: UK and EU publish a statement about the Brexit deal and plan a summit
levels.body:
The UK and the European Union have published a joint statement about the deal that took the UK out of the EU. A group called the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee agreed it on 10 November. Its job is to check that both sides are keeping their promises.
The statement covers the Withdrawal Agreement, the 2020 treaty about leaving, and the Windsor Framework, which sets the rules for goods moving to and from Northern Ireland. It also says an EU-UK Summit will take place on 20 November.
The government page does not say what the summit is expected to decide, so it is too early to say what changes might follow.
levels.why: The rules between the UK and the EU affect trade, prices and Northern Ireland.

levels.headline: UK and EU say they are working on Brexit deal and will meet on 20 November
levels.body:
The UK and the EU have published a joint statement after a meeting about the deal that took Britain out of the EU. It was released on 10 November by a group called the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee.
The statement is about putting two agreements into practice. One is the Withdrawal Agreement, the 2020 Brexit treaty. The other is the Windsor Framework, which sets how goods move to and from Northern Ireland. It also mentions an EU-UK Summit on 20 November.
The UK government page does not say what the summit will decide.
levels.why: It affects trade and rules for businesses and people in the UK and Northern Ireland.

levels.headline: UK and EU issue a joint statement on the Brexit deal
levels.body:
The UK and the European Union have put out a joint statement. A group that checks how the Brexit deal is working, called the Withdrawal Agreement Joint Committee, met and agreed it on 10 November.
The statement talks about two agreements. The first is the Withdrawal Agreement, the treaty from 2020 that set out how the UK would leave the EU. The second is the Windsor Framework, which decides how goods can travel to and from Northern Ireland.
The statement also says there will be a meeting between the UK and the EU on 20 November. We do not yet know what will be decided there.
levels.why: It matters because trade rules with the EU affect prices, businesses and Northern Ireland.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU are keeping in touch about Brexit
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union, which is a group of European countries, a few years ago. The two sides signed a deal about how to do it. A special group checks that both sides are following the deal. It met this month and put out a statement on 10 November.
The statement is about two things. One is the exit deal itself, called the Withdrawal Agreement. The other is the Windsor Framework, a set of rules for goods going to and from Northern Ireland.
The statement also says the UK and the EU will hold a summit, which is a big meeting, on 20 November. We do not yet know what will be agreed.
levels.why: The rules between the UK and the EU affect the cost and ease of trade.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU say they will meet on 20 November
levels.body:
The UK used to be in the European Union, a club of European countries. It left a few years ago. The two sides signed a deal about how to split up. A small group checks they are both keeping to it.
That group met and put out a short statement on 10 November. It talked about the exit deal and also about the Windsor Framework. That is a set of rules for goods going into and out of Northern Ireland.
The statement also says the UK and EU will have a big meeting on 20 November. It does not say what they will decide. We will have to wait and see.
levels.why: These rules affect the price of goods and how easy it is to trade.

levels.headline: The UK and the EU will have a big meeting
levels.body:
The UK used to be part of the European Union, a group of European countries. When it left, the two sides made a deal to say who does what. A little group checks that both sides follow it. They met this month.
They wrote a short note on 10 November. It talks about the leaving deal. It also talks about rules for goods that go to Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK but shares a border with Ireland, a country in the EU.
The note also says there will be a big meeting between the UK and the EU on 20 November. We do not know yet what they will say.
levels.why: It can change how easy and cheap it is to trade with Europe.

levels.headline: The UK and its European neighbours will meet
levels.body:
The UK left a group of European countries, called the European Union. Before it left, the UK and the group made a deal about how to part. Now a small team checks that both sides stick to the deal. It is like two schools agreeing rules for a shared field.
The team met and wrote a note on 10 November. The note says the UK and the EU will hold a big meeting on 20 November. We do not know what they will talk about or decide.
The note also mentions Northern Ireland, which has special rules for goods that cross its border.
levels.why: The rules between countries can change the price of things in shops.

levels.headline: The UK and its neighbours have a meeting coming up
levels.body:
Imagine two schools that share a playground. They agree some rules about who plays where, and sometimes they check that everyone is following them.
The UK and a group of its neighbours called the European Union have a deal like that. It was made when the UK left the group. A small team met and wrote a note about it on 10 November. The note says the UK and the EU will hold a big meeting on 20 November. Nobody knows yet what they will decide.
The note also talks about Northern Ireland, a part of the UK that has special rules for goods crossing its border.
levels.why: The deal can make it easier or harder to buy things from our neighbours.

headline: EU leaders add Italy and Poland to Ukraine peace talks team instead of naming a single envoy

terms.meaning: A person sent to represent a country or group in talks.
Penalties, usually economic, imposed on a country.

levels.headline: EU leaders add Italy and Poland to Ukraine peace talks team instead of naming a single envoy
levels.body:
EU leaders meeting in Dublin on 13 November did not appoint a single envoy to speak for Europe in Ukraine peace talks. Instead they widened the existing negotiating group, adding Italy and Poland. The joint team now comprises France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, with the European Council, European Commission and NATO also represented.
The decision leaves EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas without the role she had sought. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said 'we always include Italy and Poland'. US envoy Jared Kushner said the deal cannot be concluded without Europeans at the table, and Zelenskyy said they will take part in the next round.
The Kremlin played down the prospect of Europe joining. Ursula von der Leyen will present a paper on Ukraine's 2027 funding and a 22nd sanctions package at a special summit on 26-27 November.
levels.why: Who speaks for Europe will shape any peace deal and the security of the whole continent.

levels.headline: EU widens Ukraine peace team to include Italy and Poland, passing over Kallas
levels.body:
EU leaders in Dublin on 13 November opted to enlarge the group representing Europe in Ukraine peace talks rather than choose one envoy. Italy and Poland join France, Germany and the UK, and the EU institutions and NATO will also be represented.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who wanted the envoy job, said 'Russians do not want me'. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany would not give up its seat for a single envoy. Giorgia Meloni had argued for one voice.
US envoy Jared Kushner said Europeans must be 'at the table', and Zelenskyy said they will join the next round. The Kremlin played this down. A special summit on 26-27 November will consider funding for Ukraine in 2027 and a 22nd sanctions package.
levels.why: The format of talks will influence what any deal looks like and how secure Europe is.

levels.headline: European leaders choose a bigger team, not one envoy, for Ukraine talks
levels.body:
European leaders met in Dublin on 13 November to decide who should speak for Europe in talks to end the war in Ukraine. They did not pick one person. They added Italy and Poland to the group that already included France, Germany and the UK. The EU and NATO are also represented.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, had wanted the job and was left out. Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Germany would keep its seat. The US envoy Jared Kushner said the deal cannot be done without Europe, and Ukraine's president said Europeans will take part in the next round of talks. The Kremlin played that down.
levels.why: Europe's role in the talks matters for the continent's future security.

levels.headline: EU leaders add two countries to the Ukraine peace talks team
levels.body:
Leaders from across Europe met in Dublin on 13 November. They had to decide who would speak for Europe in talks about ending the war in Ukraine. They did not choose one person. They added Italy and Poland to a team that already had France, Germany and the UK. The EU and NATO are in the team too.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wanted the role but did not get it. She said the Russians do not want her. The US envoy Jared Kushner said the deal needs Europeans at the table. Ukraine's leader said Europe will join the next talks. Russia's government said little about this.
levels.why: It decides who has a say about the future of Ukraine and Europe's safety.

levels.headline: European leaders pick a bigger team, not one envoy, for talks on ending the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
European leaders met in Dublin on 13 November to decide who should speak for Europe in talks about ending the war in Ukraine. They chose a team of countries rather than one person. Italy and Poland joined France, Germany and the UK, and the EU and NATO will be represented too.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, did not get the role she wanted. The US envoy Jared Kushner said a deal cannot be reached without Europeans at the table. Ukraine's president said they will join the next round, but the Kremlin played that down.
A special EU summit on 26 and 27 November will look at how to pay for Ukraine's needs in 2027 and at a 22nd package of sanctions on Russia.
levels.why: Europe's role in the talks affects how the war ends and how safe the continent is.

levels.headline: European countries agree a team for the Ukraine peace talks
levels.body:
European leaders met in Dublin on 13 November. They wanted to decide who should speak for Europe in talks about ending the war in Ukraine. In the end they did not pick one person. They picked a team of countries: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK. The EU and NATO will also be there.
One woman, Kaja Kallas, who looks after the EU's work with other countries, had wanted to lead. She did not get the job. A US envoy said a deal cannot be made without Europe. Ukraine's president said Europe will join the next round of talks. Russia said little to welcome that.
levels.why: Who is at the table can decide how the war ends and how safe Europe is.

levels.headline: Europe chooses a team for the talks about the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
A war has been going on in Ukraine, after Russia attacked it. Now countries are holding talks to try to end it. Until now, Europe was not sitting at the table. This week, European leaders met in Dublin to decide how Europe should join.
They did not choose one person. They chose a team of countries instead: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK. A woman called Kaja Kallas had hoped to lead but did not get the job.
A US envoy, Jared Kushner, said a deal cannot be made without Europe. Ukraine's president said Europe will join the next round. Russia did not seem keen.
levels.why: The talks decide how a war in Europe ends, so it matters who takes part.

levels.headline: European countries pick a team for the Ukraine peace talks
levels.body:
There is a war in Ukraine. Russia attacked Ukraine, and many people have been hurt. Some countries are talking about how to stop it. Europe wants a place at the table.
On 13 November, leaders from many European countries met in Dublin. They did not choose just one person to speak for Europe. They chose a team of countries instead. These are France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK.
A woman called Kaja Kallas wanted the job, but she did not get it. A man from the US said it is not possible to make a deal without Europe. Russia did not say it was happy about it. Europe's leaders will meet again in two weeks.
levels.why: It matters because it decides who helps shape the end of the war.

levels.headline: Europe picks a team to help end the war in Ukraine
levels.body:
There is a war in Ukraine. A big country called Russia attacked a smaller one. Some other countries are talking about how to make it stop. They are holding peace talks. Until now, Europe was not at the table.
On 13 November, leaders from European countries met in a city called Dublin. They had to choose who would speak for Europe. A team is better than one person, they thought, so they chose five countries: France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK.
A man from the US said Europe must be at the table. Russia did not sound happy. Everyone hopes the talks will help end the war.
levels.why: It matters because everyone wants the war to end, and Europe wants a say.

levels.headline: Europe picks a team for the peace talks
levels.body:
Imagine two groups in the playground are having a big argument. Other children want to help sort it out. They hold a meeting to say how to stop it. That is what peace talks are.
There is a war in Ukraine. Many countries are trying to help end it. Europe wants a place at the meeting. On 13 November its leaders met and chose a team of countries to speak for them. They chose the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
They did not choose just one child to speak. They chose a team, so more voices can be heard. A man from the US said Europe should be at the table. Many people hope the war will end soon.
levels.why: It matters because everyone hopes the fighting in Ukraine will stop.

headline: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang steps down and agrees to testify to Congress

terms.meaning: Temporary, until a permanent replacement is found.
A legal order requiring someone to give evidence.

levels.headline: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang steps down and agrees to testify to Congress
levels.body:
Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday 12 November. The chipmaker named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive, and told CNBC it had not yet chosen a search firm to find a permanent successor.
The exit followed the board opening an investigation into Huang's relationship with a businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast said Huang had agreed to testify, likely before Thanksgiving, and would be subpoenaed if needed. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has reportedly agreed to testify to the Senate Banking Committee about chip sales to China.
levels.why: Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies, so its leadership and China links affect markets and US-China relations.

levels.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns as chief executive amid China spy row
levels.body:
Jensen Huang left his post as Nvidia chief executive on 12 November. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and the board has not yet picked a search firm for a permanent replacement, it told CNBC.
The board had opened an inquiry into Huang's relationship with a businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies describe as a Chinese spy. Nvidia has retained the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that he was targeted by foreign intelligence.
House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast said Huang has agreed to testify, probably before Thanksgiving. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has reportedly agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee about chip sales to China.
levels.why: The company sits at the centre of the AI boom, so the row affects investors and US-China tensions.

levels.headline: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang steps down
levels.body:
Jensen Huang has stepped down as chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia. The move came on 12 November. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will act as chief executive for now, and the company has not yet chosen how to find a permanent replacement.
The board had been investigating Huang's relationship with a businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to look into claims that he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
A senior US congressman, Brian Mast, said Huang has agreed to testify to Congress. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has reportedly agreed to testify to a Senate committee too.
levels.why: Nvidia is hugely valuable, so what happens to it can move markets and US-China relations.

levels.headline: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang leaves the company
levels.body:
The chief executive of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has left the job. He stepped down on 12 November. The company's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will run it for now as interim chief executive. Nvidia says it has not yet chosen a firm to help find a permanent replacement.
The board had been looking into his relationship with a businesswoman whom US spy agencies say works for China. Nvidia has hired a law firm, Wachtell Lipton, to investigate.
A US politician, Brian Mast, said Huang has agreed to speak to Congress and will probably do so before Thanksgiving. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has reportedly agreed to speak to a Senate committee about chip sales to China.
levels.why: Nvidia is one of the biggest firms in the world, so its troubles can shake stock markets.

levels.headline: The boss of chip company Nvidia has left
levels.body:
Jensen Huang, the boss of the chip company Nvidia, has stepped down. This happened on 12 November. Nvidia makes computer chips that are used in artificial intelligence. For now, a senior manager called Colette Kress is in charge. This is called an interim role, which means it is for a short time.
The company's board had been looking into Huang's links with a woman whom US spy agencies say is a Chinese spy. Nvidia has hired lawyers to investigate.
A member of the US Congress said Huang has agreed to answer questions, likely before Thanksgiving. The US Commerce Secretary has also reportedly agreed to answer questions about chips sold to China.
levels.why: Nvidia is huge, so changes there can affect share prices and relations between the US and China.

levels.headline: The chief of chip firm Nvidia has stepped down
levels.body:
Jensen Huang has stepped down as boss of Nvidia, a firm that makes computer chips used for artificial intelligence. It happened on 12 November. A manager called Colette Kress is in charge for now. That is called an interim role, which means a short-term one.
The firm's leaders had been looking into his friendship with a woman whom US spy agencies say is a Chinese spy. The firm has hired lawyers to find out more.
The US Congress wants to ask him questions. A senior member said he has agreed to answer them. The US Commerce Secretary will also be questioned about chips sold to China.
levels.why: Nvidia is so big that its news can move share prices and affect how the US and China get on.

levels.headline: The head of a big chip company has stepped down
levels.body:
The boss of a very big company called Nvidia has left his job. His name is Jensen Huang. Nvidia makes computer chips that help power artificial intelligence. He left on 12 November.
A senior manager, Colette Kress, will run the company for now. The company's leaders had been looking into his friendship with a woman that US spy agencies say is a spy for China. They have asked lawyers to find out more.
A member of the US Congress, which is where US laws are made, said Huang has agreed to answer questions. The US Commerce Secretary may do so too. They want to know about chips sold to China.
levels.why: Nvidia is so big that its news can change share prices and how countries get on.

levels.headline: The boss of a chip company has left his job
levels.body:
A man called Jensen Huang was the boss of a very big company called Nvidia. It makes computer chips. Many smart computer programs use these chips. On 12 November he left his job.
The people in charge of the company had been looking into his friendship with a woman. US spy agencies say she is a spy for China. A spy secretly gets information for another country. The company has asked lawyers to find out what happened.
A woman called Colette Kress is in charge for now. The man has agreed to answer questions from US politicians. They want to be sure that important computer chips do not go to the wrong place.
levels.why: Nvidia is so big that this news made share prices go down.

levels.headline: A big chip company has a new temporary boss
levels.body:
A very big company called Nvidia makes the special chips that smart computers use. Its boss, Jensen Huang, has left his job. This happened on 12 November. A woman called Colette Kress is now in charge for a short time.
The company's leaders were worried about his friendship with a woman. US spy agencies say she is a spy, which means someone who secretly finds out things for another country. The company has asked lawyers to look into it.
The people who make rules for America want to ask him questions. He has said yes. They want to know that important chips do not end up somewhere they should not.
levels.why: The company is so big that its news can change share prices.

levels.headline: The head of a big chip company has stepped back
levels.body:
Nvidia is a company that makes tiny computer chips. These chips are like the brains inside smart computers. Its boss, Jensen Huang, has stepped down from his job. He did it on 12 November.
The people who run the company were worried about a friendship he had. US officials say the woman is a spy for another country. A spy is someone who secretly gets information. The company has asked lawyers to find out what happened.
For now, a woman called Colette Kress is in charge, like a stand-in teacher. The boss has said he will answer questions from American politicians, who make the country's rules.
levels.why: It matters because Nvidia is so big that changes there can affect many people's savings.

headline: Brent crude heads for second weekly fall near $95 as Trump keeps Iran blockade

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
Stopping ships or goods from entering or leaving a place.

levels.headline: Brent crude heads for second weekly fall near $95 as Trump keeps Iran blockade
levels.body:
Brent crude traded at about $95 to $96 a barrel on 13 November, and CNBC said it was set for a second weekly decline, of about 2.4%, after falling 16% the week before. Trading Economics put Brent at $96.08.
Prices dropped earlier in the week on hopes of diplomacy over the Iran war. They rose on 12 November after President Donald Trump said a deal with Iran was not needed to end the war, suggesting the US blockade on oil shipments and sanctions will stay in place. Attacks on tankers and shipping in the Gulf keep a risk premium in the market.
One analyst warned that Trump's claim that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz could provoke more Iranian attacks on shipping.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, energy bills and inflation, which in turn influence interest rate decisions.

levels.headline: Oil heads for a second weekly drop as US keeps Iran blockade
levels.body:
Brent crude was trading around $95 to $96 a barrel on 13 November. CNBC said it was set for a 2.4% fall over the week, following a 16% plunge the week before.
Prices had dipped on hopes of a diplomatic solution to the Iran war, then rose after President Trump said a deal was not needed to end it, which suggests the blockade on Iranian oil shipments and sanctions will continue. Attacks on tankers in the Gulf have kept a risk premium in prices.
An analyst warned that Trump's statement that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz could provoke further Iranian attacks on shipping.
levels.why: Oil is a key driver of inflation, so it influences the cost of living and interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall for a second week but stay high
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main global oil price, was about $95 to $96 a barrel on 13 November. It was on course for a second weekly fall, of around 2.4%, after dropping 16% the week before, CNBC reported.
Prices fell on hopes of peace talks over the Iran war, but rose again after President Trump said the US does not need a deal to end the war. That suggests his blockade on Iranian oil, and sanctions, will carry on. Attacks on ships in the Gulf also keep prices higher.
An analyst warned that Trump's claim that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route, might lead to more Iranian attacks.
levels.why: Higher oil prices push up fuel costs and prices in shops, which affects family budgets.

levels.headline: Oil heads for another weekly fall but is still around $95
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main global price for oil, was around $95 to $96 a barrel on 13 November. It is on track to fall for the second week in a row. Last week it fell 16%, and this week it looks set to fall about 2.4%, CNBC reported.
Prices dipped when people hoped the war involving Iran might end through talks. They rose again after President Trump said a deal was not needed, which means the American blockade of Iranian oil is likely to stay. Attacks on ships near the Gulf also keep prices up.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea route that much of the world's oil passes through.
levels.why: Oil prices affect petrol, heating bills and the price of many goods.

levels.headline: Oil prices have gone down again this week, but not by much
levels.body:
Oil is still costing about $95 to $96 a barrel on 13 November. That is the price of Brent crude, which is used as a world guide. It has gone down for the second week running. Last week it fell by a big 16%. This week it is down about 2.4%.
The war involving Iran has been pushing oil prices around. Prices fell when people hoped for peace talks. They went up again when the US President, Donald Trump, said a deal was not needed. That means a US blockade of Iranian oil will probably go on. Ships in the Gulf have also been attacked.
Much of the world's oil goes through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz.
levels.why: Oil costs affect petrol prices and the cost of living.

levels.headline: Oil is still dear, though it has fallen again this week
levels.body:
Oil was about $95 to $96 a barrel on 13 November. It has now fallen for two weeks in a row, but it is still dear. Brent crude is the price most of the world uses as a guide.
The main reason is the war involving Iran. Prices dropped when people hoped for peace talks. They rose after the US President said a deal was not needed, which means the US blockade of Iranian oil will probably stay. Ships in the Gulf have also been attacked.
Much of the world's oil travels through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route near Iran, so any trouble there can quickly change prices.
levels.why: When oil is dear, fuel and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs a bit less than last week, but it is still dear
levels.body:
Oil costs about $95 to $96 for a barrel on 13 November. A barrel is a big container. Oil has got a bit cheaper for the second week in a row. Last week it fell a lot. This week it fell a little.
There is a war involving Iran. Prices go down when people hope for peace and go up when they fear more trouble. This week, the US President said the US does not need a deal. So the US will keep stopping ships carrying oil from Iran. Ships near the Gulf have also been attacked.
Oil is used to make petrol and many other things.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and many other things cost more too.

levels.headline: Oil is cheaper than last week but still costs a lot
levels.body:
Oil costs about 95 dollars for a big barrel. It was a bit cheaper this week than last week. It has gone down two weeks in a row. But it is still dear.
The reason is a war involving Iran. Iran is near a narrow sea path that lots of the world's oil ships use. When people hope for peace, the price goes down. When they worry about more fighting, it goes up. This week, the US President said the US does not need a deal. The US will keep stopping oil ships from Iran. Some ships nearby have been attacked.
Oil is used to make petrol and many things in shops.
levels.why: If oil costs more, petrol and shop prices can go up.

levels.headline: Oil costs less than last week but is still pricey
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid from under the ground. People make petrol from it. Oil costs about 95 dollars a barrel now. That is a bit less than last week and the week before.
There is a war that involves a country called Iran. Ships carry oil near it. When people hope for peace, the price goes down. When they worry, it goes up. This week the US President said the US will keep stopping ships carrying Iran's oil. That keeps people a little worried.
When oil costs a lot, petrol costs a lot too. Then lots of things in the shops can cost more.
levels.why: If oil costs a lot, petrol and many other things cost more.

levels.headline: The price of oil is still high
levels.body:
Oil is what makes petrol for cars. It is also used to make plastic and many other things. People buy and sell it by the barrel, a big container. Now a barrel costs about 95 dollars.
It is a bit cheaper than last week. But it is still pricey. There is a war far away, near a country called Iran. A lot of the world's oil travels in ships near there. When people worry about the ships, the price goes up, like a toy getting dearer when everybody wants it.
When oil costs a lot, petrol costs a lot, and shops may put their prices up.
levels.why: If oil is dear, many things cost more, and that is hard for families.

headline: Representation of the People Bill reaches House of Lords committee stage

terms.meaning: A stage where peers examine a bill line by line and propose changes.
The UK Parliament's second chamber, which checks and revises laws.

levels.headline: Representation of the People Bill reaches House of Lords committee stage
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has entered its committee stage in the House of Lords, according to a government blog post dated 2 November. Among its measures is the extension of the vote to 16 and 17-year-olds. It also includes a cap of £100,000 a year on donations from overseas electors.
Committee stage is when peers examine a bill in detail, clause by clause, and can propose changes. It comes after the bill has been debated in principle and before it returns to the full House for further stages. The blog post does not say when it will be passed or become law.
The bill is part of the government's plan to change how elections are run and funded in the UK.
levels.why: It could change who is allowed to vote and how political parties are funded.

levels.headline: Votes at 16 bill moves into detailed scrutiny in the Lords
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill is now at committee stage in the House of Lords, a government blog from 2 November says. The bill would give 16 and 17-year-olds the vote and cap donations from overseas electors at £100,000 a year.
At committee stage, peers go through the bill line by line and can suggest amendments. After this the bill returns to the full chamber for further stages. The blog does not give a date for completion.
The bill is part of the government's changes to how elections are run and how political parties are funded.
levels.why: Lowering the voting age and limiting donations would alter who takes part in elections and how they are paid for.

levels.headline: A bill to give 16-year-olds the vote is now being examined in the Lords
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote is now at committee stage in the House of Lords, a government blog said on 2 November. It is called the Representation of the People Bill.
The bill would also cap donations from overseas voters at £100,000 a year. Committee stage is where members of the Lords go through a bill line by line and suggest changes. Later, the bill goes back to the whole House.
The blog does not say when the bill will finish its journey through Parliament or when it could become law. It is part of the government's plans to change election rules.
levels.why: It could change who can vote and how political parties are funded.

levels.headline: Lords start detailed checks on bill to lower the voting age
levels.body:
The House of Lords has started examining a bill that would lower the voting age to 16. The bill is called the Representation of the People Bill. A government blog post on 2 November said it has reached committee stage in the Lords.
The bill would also limit the amount that people living overseas can donate to political parties to £100,000 a year. At committee stage, members of the Lords go through the bill carefully and can suggest changes. It then goes back to the full House.
No date has been given for when the bill might become law.
levels.why: It could change who can vote and where party money comes from.

levels.headline: Lords begin close examination of bill to lower voting age to 16
levels.body:
A bill to let 16 and 17-year-olds vote has reached the House of Lords, according to a government blog post on 2 November. The Representation of the People Bill is at committee stage, when peers read it line by line and can suggest changes.
The bill would also set a limit of £100,000 a year on donations from overseas electors to political parties. After committee stage the bill goes back to the whole House for more stages.
The blog does not say when the process will end or when the changes could take effect. The bill is part of the government's plans to change how elections work in the UK.
levels.why: It could change who can vote and where political parties get their money.

levels.headline: A law to let 16-year-olds vote is being checked in the Lords
levels.body:
A new law is being looked at in Parliament. It would let people aged 16 and 17 vote in elections. At the moment you must be 18 to vote in most UK elections. The new law is called the Representation of the People Bill.
The bill has reached the House of Lords. That is the part of Parliament where members check laws carefully. This stage is called committee stage. The Lords go through the bill line by line and can suggest changes.
The bill would also limit gifts of money to political parties from voters who live abroad. The limit would be £100,000 a year.
levels.why: It could change who is allowed to vote and how parties get their money.

levels.headline: The Lords are looking at a law about voting at 16
levels.body:
The UK might change who can vote. Now you must be 18 in most elections. A new law, called a bill, would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote. A bill is an idea for a law that has to go through Parliament.
The bill is now in the House of Lords, where people check it carefully. They go through it bit by bit and say what could be changed.
The bill would also limit how much money people living abroad can give to political parties. The limit is £100,000 a year. We do not yet know when the bill will become law.
levels.why: It could let millions of young people vote for the first time.

levels.headline: The Lords are checking a law that would let 16-year-olds vote
levels.body:
In the UK, you have to be 18 to vote in most elections. A new idea for a law, called a bill, would let people aged 16 and 17 vote too. For a bill to become a law, it must go through Parliament.
The bill is now in a part of Parliament called the House of Lords. The people there read the bill very carefully and say what might need to change.
The bill would also limit how much money people living abroad can give to political parties. The limit would be £100,000 a year. We do not yet know when it might become a law.
levels.why: It could mean young people get a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A bill to let 16-year-olds vote is being checked
levels.body:
In the UK, you need to be 18 to vote in most elections. People in charge want to change that. They want 16-year-olds to vote too. They have written an idea for a new law, called a bill.
A bill must be checked carefully before it becomes a law. Now a group of grown-ups in the House of Lords, which is part of Parliament, are going through it slowly. They read each part and can ask for changes.
The bill also says that people who live far away cannot give too much money to political parties. The most they can give is £100,000 a year.
levels.why: It could mean young people get a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are checking a plan to let 16-year-olds vote
levels.body:
Voting is how people choose who runs the country. Today you have to be 18 to vote in most elections. A new plan would let 16-year-olds join in. The plan is called a bill, and it has to be checked before it can become a law.
The checking is happening in a place called the House of Lords. The people there read the plan carefully, a bit like a teacher checking a long piece of homework, and say what might need to change.
The plan also says that political parties cannot take too much money from people who live far away.
levels.why: If it becomes law, young people could have a say in who runs the country.

headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing and living costs

terms.meaning: A strike by workers across many industries at once.
An election called earlier than scheduled.

levels.headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing and living costs
levels.body:
Spain's two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, held a 24-hour national general strike on 11 November, the first in 14 years, according to CNBC. It disrupted transport and businesses and formed part of a wave of protests over housing and the cost of living.
The unrest follows parliament voting down emergency decrees meant to protect tenants. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then called a snap election for 29 November, and his government approved 21 urgent housing measures. The opposition People's Party called the strike an election strike, and the government did not officially endorse it.
The Bank of Spain estimates a shortage of 750,000 homes. Housing prices rose 12.2% year on year in the second quarter, while wages rose by about 3% to 4%.
levels.why: Housing costs are straining households across Europe and are now shaping the result of a national election.

levels.headline: Spain's first general strike in 14 years hits transport and business
levels.body:
Spain's biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, called a 24-hour general strike on 11 November, the first in 14 years, CNBC reported. Transport and businesses were disrupted as part of protests over housing and the cost of living.
It follows parliament rejecting emergency tenant-protection decrees. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for 29 November and approved 21 urgent housing measures. The People's Party called the strike an election strike.
The Bank of Spain estimates a shortfall of 750,000 homes. House prices rose 12.2% in the year to the second quarter, but wages rose only 3% to 4%.
levels.why: The housing squeeze is becoming a major political issue ahead of the 29 November election.

levels.headline: Spain holds a national strike over housing costs
levels.body:
Workers across Spain went on strike for 24 hours on 11 November. It was Spain's first general strike in 14 years. The unions UGT and CCOO called it, and transport and businesses were disrupted, CNBC said.
People are angry about how expensive housing has become. Parliament recently voted down emergency rules to protect tenants. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then called an early election for 29 November and announced 21 urgent housing measures. The main opposition party called the strike an election strike.
The Bank of Spain thinks the country is 750,000 homes short. House prices rose 12.2% in a year, but wages rose by only about 3% to 4%.
levels.why: Housing costs are a big issue for voters and may decide the election.

levels.headline: Spain's workers strike over housing and the cost of living
levels.body:
Millions of workers in Spain stopped work for a day on 11 November. This was a general strike, where workers from many different jobs strike at once. It was the first in Spain for 14 years. Two big unions called it, and transport and businesses were affected.
The workers are angry because homes cost so much. Parliament recently voted down emergency rules to protect people who rent. The Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has called an early election for 29 November and announced 21 new housing measures.
The Bank of Spain says the country is short of 750,000 homes. Prices went up 12.2% in a year, but wages rose by much less.
levels.why: It shows how housing costs can shape politics and elections.

levels.headline: Spain's workers hold a national strike over the cost of housing
levels.body:
Workers across Spain went on strike for a day on 11 November. It was a general strike, which means people from many different jobs stop work together. It was the first in Spain for 14 years, and it was called by the unions UGT and CCOO.
The workers are angry about housing. Rents and house prices have risen far faster than pay. House prices went up 12.2% in a year, but wages rose only about 3% to 4%. The Bank of Spain says the country is short of 750,000 homes.
The Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has called an early election for 29 November and announced 21 urgent housing measures.
levels.why: Housing costs are hitting families, and they are now a big issue in politics.

levels.headline: Spain has a big strike about housing costs
levels.body:
On 11 November, workers all over Spain stopped work for the day. This is called a general strike. It means people from many different jobs strike together. It was the first one in Spain for 14 years. Trains, buses and shops were affected.
Why? Homes in Spain cost far too much for many people. Rents and prices have gone up much faster than pay. The Bank of Spain says the country is short of 750,000 homes.
Parliament voted down some rules to help renters. Then the Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, called an early election for 29 November. He also announced 21 new ideas to help with housing.
levels.why: High housing costs hurt families, and they are now an important part of politics.

levels.headline: Workers in Spain strike because homes cost too much
levels.body:
On 11 November, lots of workers in Spain did not go to work. They went on strike for a day. When workers from many different jobs strike together, it is called a general strike. It had not happened in Spain for 14 years.
Why did they do it? Homes cost too much. House prices went up by 12% in a year. But pay only went up by about 3% or 4%. So many people cannot afford to rent or buy. Spain also needs about 750,000 more homes.
The Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has called an early election for 29 November. He has promised 21 new ideas to help.
levels.why: It shows how much housing costs matter to ordinary people.

levels.headline: People in Spain went on strike about the cost of homes
levels.body:
On 11 November, many people in Spain did not go to work. They stayed away on purpose to show they were angry. That is called a strike. This one was very big because people from many jobs joined. It was the first time in 14 years.
They are angry because homes cost so much. A home costs about 12% more than a year ago. But people's pay has gone up by only a few pence in every pound. Spain also needs 750,000 more homes.
The Prime Minister has called an election for 29 November. He says he has 21 ideas to help.
levels.why: Homes that cost too much are a problem for families and for the country.

levels.headline: People in Spain stopped work to say homes cost too much
levels.body:
