On 11 November, lots of people in Spain stopped work for the day. They did this to show they are upset. This kind of big strike had not happened in Spain for 14 years.
They are upset because homes cost too much money. It is like if the price of a sweet went up a lot, but your pocket money did not. Many families cannot find a home they can afford. Spain also needs 750,000 more homes.
The leader of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has called an election for 29 November. That is when people vote for who should run the country. He says he has 21 ideas to help.
levels.why: If homes cost too much, many families struggle to find a place to live.

levels.headline: People in Spain stopped work because homes cost too much
levels.body:
Imagine all the grown-ups in your town stopped going to work for one day. They did it to say, 'We are not happy!' That is called a strike. It happened in Spain on 11 November, and it was the biggest kind of strike.
They are upset because homes cost too much. It is like if sweets got much dearer but pocket money stayed the same. Lots of families cannot find a home they can pay for.
The leader of Spain has called a vote for 29 November. That is when people choose who should lead. He says he has 21 ideas to help with homes.
levels.why: It matters because everybody needs a home that they can afford.

headline: EU spent an estimated €8.7bn on Russian Arctic LNG in 2026 as import ban looms

terms.meaning: Liquefied natural gas, gas cooled into a liquid so ships can carry it.
A rule that stops a product being brought into a country.

levels.headline: EU spent an estimated €8.7bn on Russian Arctic LNG in 2026 as import ban looms
levels.body:
The EU spent about €8.7bn on Russian Arctic liquefied natural gas (LNG) in the first ten months of 2026, according to an analysis by the campaign group Urgewald, reported by Euronews. That is 21% more than its estimate for the whole of 2025.
The figures use Kpler shipping data, which show EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes of LNG from Russia's Yamal project between January and October. The rise reflects both higher volumes and more expensive gas.
The EU's 19th sanctions package bans Russian LNG imports from 1 January 2027, though questions remain over enforcement. Russia's Alexander Novak said companies will redirect some LNG to other markets. The €8.7bn is Urgewald's estimate, not an official EU figure.
levels.why: The spending helps fund Russia while Europe tries to end its energy dependence on it.

levels.headline: EU's Russian Arctic LNG bill reaches an estimated €8.7bn ahead of ban
levels.body:
Campaign group Urgewald estimates that the EU paid about €8.7bn for Russian Arctic LNG between January and October 2026, 21% more than for all of 2025, Euronews reported. It is Urgewald's estimate rather than an official EU number.
Based on Kpler data, EU ports took 12.89 million tonnes from Russia's Yamal project in the period. Higher volumes and higher prices both pushed up the bill.
The 19th sanctions package bans Russian LNG imports from 1 January 2027, but doubts remain about enforcement without exemptions. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak says firms will redirect some LNG elsewhere.
levels.why: It shows how hard it is for Europe to cut energy ties with Russia.

levels.headline: EU spending on Russian Arctic gas rises before the ban
levels.body:
The EU spent about €8.7bn on liquefied natural gas from Russia's Arctic in the first ten months of 2026, the campaign group Urgewald estimates. Euronews reported that this is 21% more than the group's estimate for the whole of 2025. It is not an official EU figure.
Shipping data shows EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes of gas from Russia's Yamal project from January to October. The bill rose because of both bigger volumes and higher prices.
A ban on Russian LNG imports is due on 1 January 2027, but some doubt it will be enforced fully. Russia says it will sell more gas elsewhere.
levels.why: It affects how much money Russia receives and how secure Europe's energy supply is.

levels.headline: EU buys more Russian Arctic gas than last year, with ban due in 2027
levels.body:
The EU has spent an estimated €8.7bn on Russian Arctic gas in the first ten months of 2026, according to the campaign group Urgewald. That is 21% more than its estimate for the whole of 2025. It is the group's estimate and not an official EU number.
The gas is called LNG, which is natural gas cooled into a liquid so ships can carry it. EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes from Russia's Yamal project. The bill rose because of larger volumes and higher prices.
The EU will ban Russian LNG from 1 January 2027, but some people doubt it will be fully enforced. Russia says it will redirect gas to other buyers.
levels.why: It shows how hard it is for Europe to end its energy ties with Russia.

levels.headline: EU keeps buying Russian Arctic gas as ban approaches
levels.body:
The EU spent about €8.7bn on gas from Russia's Arctic in 2026 up to October. This figure is an estimate by a campaign group called Urgewald. It is 21% more than the group's estimate for all of 2025.
The gas is called LNG, which means it was cooled into a liquid so ships can carry it. EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes of it from Russia's Yamal project between January and October. The bill went up because there was more gas, and because gas was more expensive.
From 1 January 2027, the EU plans to ban Russian LNG. Some people doubt that it will be enforced without exceptions.
levels.why: It means money keeps flowing to Russia while the EU tries to end this trade.

levels.headline: The EU has spent billions on Russian gas this year
levels.body:
The EU has spent about €8.7bn on gas from Russia's Arctic this year, up to October. That is an estimate from a campaign group called Urgewald. It is 21% more than they think was spent in all of last year.
The gas is called LNG. It is cooled into a liquid so that ships can carry it. Ships brought 12.89 million tonnes of it to EU ports in ten months. The bill grew because there was more gas and because the price was higher.
The EU has made a rule to stop buying this gas from 1 January 2027. Some people worry it will not really be enforced.
levels.why: It matters because the money helps Russia, which is at war with Ukraine.

levels.headline: The EU is still buying lots of gas from Russia
levels.body:
Gas is used for heating homes and making power. The EU has been buying a lot of it from Russia's cold north, the Arctic. A campaign group called Urgewald thinks the EU paid about €8.7bn for it this year. That is more than last year.
The gas travels on ships, so it is cooled into a liquid. This kind of gas is called LNG. Ships brought lots of it to Europe. The price went up too.
The EU has a rule that will stop this from 1 January 2027. Some people worry it will not really happen. Russia says it will sell its gas to other places.
levels.why: The money helps Russia while it fights a war.

levels.headline: The EU is still buying gas from Russia
levels.body:
Many homes use gas for heat. Some of the gas used in Europe comes from Russia. The EU has spent about €8.7bn on it this year. A group that campaigns about this thinks that is more than last year. Gas costs more now, and the EU also bought more.
The gas comes by ship. It is turned into a liquid first. Then it can be carried across the sea.
The EU has said it will stop buying it from 1 January 2027. This is because Russia is fighting a war. But some people worry the EU will still find a way to buy it. Russia says it can sell to others.
levels.why: The money helps Russia while the war goes on.

levels.headline: Europe still buys gas from Russia, but wants to stop
levels.body:
Gas keeps many homes warm. Some of Europe's gas comes from Russia. This year Europe paid about €8.7bn for it. A group that campaigns about this thinks that is a lot more than last year.
The big problem is that Russia is fighting a war. The money Europe pays helps Russia. So Europe made a rule: from 1 January 2027, it will stop buying this gas.
But some people worry that the rule will not be properly kept. It is a bit like saying you will stop eating sweets next year, but still having some now. Russia says it will sell to other places instead.
levels.why: It matters because the money helps Russia while it fights a war.

levels.headline: Europe still buys gas from Russia, though it wants to stop
levels.body:
Imagine your family wants to stop buying sweets from a shop you do not like. You make a rule: no more sweets from there, starting in January. But until January, you keep buying some.
That is a bit like what Europe is doing. It buys gas from Russia, which is fighting a war. This year it paid about €8.7bn. A group that campaigns about this thinks that is more than last year.
Europe has made a rule to stop from 1 January 2027. But some people worry the rule will not be kept. Russia says it will sell its gas to other places instead.
levels.why: The money helps Russia while the war goes on.

headline: Türkiye and China sign preliminary $15bn solar and wind deal at COP31

terms.meaning: A unit of power; one gigawatt can supply around a million homes' worth in some measures.
Energy from sources such as sun and wind that do not run out.

levels.headline: Türkiye and China sign preliminary $15bn solar and wind deal at COP31
levels.body:
Türkiye and China signed a preliminary deal at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya that aims to attract about $15bn of solar and wind investment, Euronews reported. It covers solar and wind farms with a combined capacity of seven gigawatts, plus energy storage and grid improvements.
The signing followed a meeting on 11 November between President Erdoğan and Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, who said Beijing would encourage more Chinese firms to invest in Türkiye. Energy minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the cooperation would include technology sharing to support domestic wind turbine production.
No timeline or financing details were given. Türkiye's solar and wind capacity was about 43.8 gigawatts at the end of September, and it aims for 175 gigawatts by 2040.
levels.why: It shows how clean energy investment is shifting, and could help Türkiye cut its reliance on fossil fuel imports.

levels.headline: China to back Turkish solar and wind with preliminary $15bn deal
levels.body:
Türkiye and China signed a preliminary agreement at COP31 in Antalya to attract around $15bn into solar and wind power, Euronews said. It includes seven gigawatts of solar and wind farms, energy storage and grid upgrades.
It followed talks on 11 November between Erdoğan and China's Vice President Han Zheng, who said Beijing would encourage more Chinese investment in Türkiye. Energy minister Alparslan Bayraktar said it would involve technology exchange to help make wind turbine equipment in Türkiye.
There is no timetable and no details on financing. Türkiye had about 43.8 gigawatts of solar and wind at the end of September and wants 175 gigawatts by 2040.
levels.why: It could speed up Türkiye's shift to clean power and deepen economic ties with China.

levels.headline: Türkiye and China agree a first step on a $15bn clean energy plan
levels.body:
Türkiye and China have signed a first agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. It aims to bring in about $15bn of investment in solar and wind power. The plan covers solar and wind farms with seven gigawatts of power in total, plus batteries and better electricity grids.
The agreement followed a meeting between Turkish President Erdoğan and China's Vice President Han Zheng. Türkiye's energy minister said it would also include sharing technology to help make wind turbines in Türkiye.
There are no dates or funding details yet. Türkiye wants to have 175 gigawatts of solar and wind by 2040, up from about 43.8 gigawatts now.
levels.why: Clean power can help cut energy costs and pollution, and the deal shows how countries are building closer economic ties.

levels.headline: Türkiye and China sign early deal to bring $15bn into solar and wind
levels.body:
Türkiye and China signed a preliminary agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. It aims to bring about $15bn of investment into solar and wind power, including farms with seven gigawatts of capacity, energy storage and a better electricity grid.
The deal followed talks on 11 November between President Erdoğan and China's Vice President Han Zheng. Türkiye's energy minister said it would include sharing technology to help make wind turbine parts in Türkiye.
No timetable or funding details have been given. Türkiye has about 43.8 gigawatts of solar and wind power and wants 175 gigawatts by 2040.
levels.why: It could help Türkiye use more clean energy and shows China's growing economic role.

levels.headline: China and Türkiye sign early deal on solar and wind power
levels.body:
China and Türkiye signed an early agreement at the COP31 climate summit, in the Turkish city of Antalya. It is meant to attract about $15bn of investment in solar and wind power. It includes new solar and wind farms with seven gigawatts of power, plus ways to store energy and improve the electricity grid.
The two countries' leaders met earlier in the week. Türkiye's energy minister said the plan would include sharing technology so Türkiye can make more of its own wind turbine parts.
There are no dates yet and no details of who will pay. Türkiye hopes to have 175 gigawatts of wind and solar by 2040.
levels.why: It shows how countries are working together on clean energy.

levels.headline: Türkiye and China agree an early plan for clean energy
levels.body:
Türkiye and China have signed a first agreement about clean energy. They did it at a big climate meeting called COP31, held in the Turkish city of Antalya. The plan is to bring in about $15bn, which is a huge amount of money, to build solar and wind power.
Solar power comes from the sun and wind power comes from moving air. Both are called renewable energy, because they do not run out. The plan covers farms with seven gigawatts of power, and also ways to store the energy.
There are no dates yet, and it is not clear who will pay. Türkiye wants a lot more solar and wind power by 2040.
levels.why: Clean energy can help the planet and lower energy costs.

levels.headline: Türkiye and China sign an early plan for sun and wind power
levels.body:
Türkiye and China have made an early agreement about clean energy. They signed it at a big climate meeting called COP31, in Antalya, a city in Türkiye.
The plan is for about $15bn to be spent on solar and wind power. Solar power uses sunlight and wind power uses moving air. They are called renewable because they never run out. The plan includes big solar and wind farms and batteries to store the power.
The plan does not say yet when it will start or who will pay. Türkiye wants to make much more solar and wind power by 2040. It also wants to learn how to make more wind turbine parts itself.
levels.why: It matters because clean energy helps the planet.

levels.headline: Türkiye and China agree a plan for clean power
levels.body:
Türkiye and China have made an early plan to make more clean power. They signed it at a big meeting about the climate, held in a city called Antalya.
Clean power comes from things that do not run out, like the sun and the wind. The plan is to spend about $15bn on solar panels and wind turbines. A wind turbine is a tall machine that spins in the wind to make electricity. The plan also includes batteries to save the power.
We do not yet know when it will start or who will pay for it. Türkiye wants lots more clean power by 2040.
levels.why: Clean power is better for the air and the planet.

levels.headline: Two countries plan to make more power from sun and wind
levels.body:
Two countries, Türkiye and China, have made a plan to make more clean power. They signed it at a big meeting about the weather and the planet, held in a city called Antalya.
Clean power comes from the sun and the wind. Solar panels catch sunlight, and wind turbines spin in the wind. These do not make dirty smoke. The plan is to spend a huge amount of money, about $15bn, on them. That is 15 billion dollars.
The plan also includes batteries to save the power. It is only a first step, so we do not know yet when it will begin.
levels.why: Clean power helps keep the air and planet healthier.

levels.headline: Two countries plan to use more sun and wind for power
levels.body:
Think of the sun shining and the wind blowing. They are free, and they never run out. We can use them to make electricity. Solar panels catch the sun and wind turbines, which look like giant windmills, catch the wind.
Two countries, Türkiye and China, have made a plan to build more of them. They signed it at a big meeting about the planet. They want to spend a huge amount of money, about $15bn.
It is only an early plan, so the details are not known yet. But more clean power means less dirty smoke in the air.
levels.why: Clean power can help keep our air and planet healthy.
